rv.q: These three shows, all flawed in very different ways, left me frustrated, ambivalent and often puzzled, but also thinking.
With its humor, emotion, and theatricality, Playing Shylock is an enriching entertainment.

Driven by a fearless curiosity and a belief in the transformative power of theater, Playing Shylock is a bracing reminder that the freedom of expression we have come to enjoy in North America is a relatively new development, and is presently slipping away in particularly stupid and insidious ways.
Saul Rubinek is compelling and achingly sincere in this thoughtful, thought-provoking one-man show on the meaning of Jewish identity on stage.
Its thoughtful and entertaining approach proves a rewarding 100 minutes.
As a result it is very necessary viewing at this time.
Given how naturally Rubinek inhabits Shylock (when opportunities to speak his lines arise), it’s surprising that he never actually played the part in a full revival of The Merchant of Venice.
Both portraits, as guided by Mr. Schechter, can take on a melodramatic quality that is, to be fair, not out of sync with Yiddish theatrical tradition...

Indeed, much of Playing Shylock's considerable entertainment value comes from fighting back in one's mind against Rubinek's broad assertions, especially his occasional tendency to make larger social trends all about himself.
some stirring and provocative moments undermined by a script rife with dubious assertions
Rubinek demonstrates an exceptional emotional range and an uncanny ability to switch from anger--cancel culture, to humor about historical assimilation pressures for Jews...

Playing Shylock deserves more of an audience, not just because of its unique take on The Merchant of Venice and antisemitism and because it stars the always wonderful Saul Rubinek; it should be seen by more Jews and goyim (non-Jews) because it’s damn good, zeyer gut.

cn.t: Saul Rubinek captivates in this timely, meta solo show about playing Shakespeare's Shylock, with critics praising his magnetic performance and the play's clever exploration of Jewish identity, antisemitism, and cancel culture.
